deepdive.sec: Industrials — Graphite Electrodes (EAF steel decarbonisation) + emerging Graphite Anode / Green Energy

bull_bear.body: HEG Limited itself is debt-free with ₹858cr of treasury and has been debt-free for years. Growth capital is going into the electrode expansion (115,000t), and — via the entity that is being demerged — into ₹2,200cr of anode capex (₹1,240cr SBI project debt, rest equity and internal accruals) plus renewable build-out. The Statkraft/Malana buy-in (~₹1,200cr, 50% bank + family office + Bhilwara Energy) leaves ₹600cr in BEL's books that management says will be retired before consolidation. Post-demerger equity structure: ~32.9cr shares in the Greentech entity versus HEG's current ~19.7-19.8cr, with ~13cr new shares to Singularity (both tranches), promoters and RSWM — and management was explicit that **no fresh issuance follows once this is routed**. Treasury is also carrying foreign equity investments whose mark-to-market swings have now materially distorted two consecutive quarters of reported profit in opposite directions.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **The price-cost lag cuts both ways.** Q1's 29% margin was helped by cheap legacy needle coke; from November-January the $200-300/t increase lands. HEG's own price increases start only in October and management explicitly cannot yet say what average increase it will achieve — "*we'll know in next 1 or 2 months.*" A margin-maintenance promise made before either side of the equation is settled is a genuine risk.
- **Peer price hikes may not stick.** Management pointedly declined to say whether GrafTech's increase is being absorbed: "*How much gets eventually absorbed by the steelmakers, that remains to be seen*". The entire H2 realisation thesis rests on announcements, not on realised prices.
- **US trade action pending, on a compressed clock.** CVD preliminary determination by end-July, anti-dumping by end-September. Exposure is <10% of volume and management is relaxed ("*We know that we have not done dumping*"), but the Chairman also conceded HEG "*might lose some sort of a market share*" in a market where "*American prices are higher than most of the others.*"
- **Structural oversupply is unresolved.** Global UHP demand is contested (an analyst put the market at ~600kt with a third Chinese; management said the Chinese share is "much less, maybe half of that"), Western utilisation sits at 60-65%, and steel industry utilisation is "*even less than 75%.*" The pricing case therefore depends on demand returning and new EAFs commissioning — both outside HEG's control.
- **Anode execution risk is now the dominant company-specific risk.** 60% of ₹2,200cr still to spend, production promised for Q1 FY28, and ~₹1,500cr of gross debt landing on the 31-Mar-27 balance sheet — on a business with no operating history, entering a market dominated by incumbent Chinese suppliers. The mitigant (70% of capacity on 3-5 year Tier-1 contracts) is itself an unconfirmed promise due within six weeks.
- **Reported profit is being distorted by treasury mark-to-market**, in both directions across Q4FY26 and Q1FY27. The "maintain 28-29% including other income" formulation embeds this.
- **Demerger timing is with the NCLT.** The order is reserved but unpronounced; record date, listing mechanics and the ~13cr share issuance all follow from it.
- **Disclosure limits.** Management explicitly refused regional volume splits, specific dollar-per-tonne contracted prices, and net spread economics on competitive-sensitivity grounds — defensible, but it makes the H2 margin promise unverifiable until it is reported.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident, senior and specific where it counts — Riju Jhunjhunwala gave a full three-year revenue and margin build for the anode business unprompted, and Puneet Anand walked through capex phasing, debt quantum and post-demerger share count without hedging. Ravi Jhunjhunwala drew clear lines on competitively sensitive disclosure ("*it is not the right forum… we have competitors all over the world*") rather than giving vague answers, and corrected an analyst's 20% US-exposure figure to 10% directly. There is some looseness: an analyst's question about "BEL debt" was answered as if it referred to HEG's own debt before being clarified as Bhilwara Energy; the anode capex figure moved between ₹2,200cr and ₹2,300cr; and the margin commitment was extracted rather than volunteered. The offer to name individual EAF customer projects offline is a good sign of genuine bottom-up demand tracking rather than citing OECD headlines.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- **The sequential earnings swing is far less dramatic than it looks.** Q4FY26's -₹126cr standalone EBITDA was driven by mark-to-market losses on foreign equity investments; Q1FY27's ₹43cr other income includes fair-valuation *gains* on the same holdings. The underlying operating recovery is real but a fraction of the -₹126cr → +₹211cr headline.
- **Volumes fell and margins expanded 600bps.** In a commodity business that is the most informative fact on the call — it says the electrode cycle has turned on price, not on demand, and that HEG's mix and cost position are doing the work.
- **The needle coke inflation is timed to hit exactly when HEG's own price increases arrive.** Both are Q3 events: HEG's book rolls off in September/October, needle coke cost lands November-January. Q2 should therefore look like Q1; the real test is Q3.
- **HEG's US "risk" is priced backwards.** The US is <10% of volume but carries the highest prices globally — so an adverse ADD/CVD outcome costs disproportionately more margin than volume. The Chairman's "*we will retain America*" reflects that asymmetry.
- **The demerger is being used to house a leveraged growth entity separately from the cash-generative core.** HEG Limited stays debt-free with ₹858cr of treasury; ~₹1,500cr of gross debt, ₹3,100cr of anode capex and the renewable build-out all sit in the entity going out — a clean risk separation that also means post-demerger the listed HEG will look very different from today's consolidated numbers.
- **Anode contracts are being locked in 3-5 year Tier-1 agreements before commissioning** — an unusually strong de-risking of a greenfield battery-materials plant, and the single item most worth verifying next quarter.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- HEG carries a sizeable treasury of investments plus cash and equivalents (excluding associates and the wholly owned subsidiary), providing internal funding capacity alongside the expansion.
- Funding leans on short-term borrowings, whose outstanding balance has trended up over the last eight quarters to roughly Rs 780-790 crore.
- The company holds an equity investment in GrafTech that is fair-valued through the P&L, so reported EBITDA can swing on mark-to-market movements unrelated to operations.
- Associate companies contribute a meaningful and growing share of consolidated pre-tax profit, indicating value held outside the standalone electrode business.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- World's largest single-site graphite electrode plant; the Company states the added tonnage deepens economies of scale that already place it in the lowest cost quartile globally
- Capacity utilisation of 90% for 2025-26 (91% per the Board's Report), stated as the highest among the peer group / among all western graphite electrode manufacturers, against a global industry average of 60-65%
- Indian cost base gives cost competitiveness through scale, economical manpower costs and a competitive cost of electrical power versus the Western world's old graphite electrode plants
- Brownfield expansion at Mandideep costs less than half the capital intensity of a greenfield plant and leverages surplus nipple capacity, the highest value-add component of the electrode
- Very high barriers to entry: no new company has entered the graphite electrode space since 1976 (ex-China) with the singular exception of HEG's Mandideep facility; most Western capacity is over 50 years old and reactivating shuttered plants is prohibitively expensive
- Long-term debt free, with a treasury of around Rs 792 Crores as of 31st March 2026
- Investment in GrafTech International held as a needle coke hedge
- Global blue-chip customer base with direct leadership engagement with the world's top 25 steel producers
- R&D division working on process optimisation and next-generation carbon materials, with strategic alliances with global research centres
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Energy cost and energy-intensity exposure — BRSR identifies Energy Management as a risk and opportunity because energy consumption constitutes a significant portion of operational costs in graphite manufacturing; inefficient energy use raises cost pressure and emissions. The MD&A calls energy markets the defining macroeconomic variable, transmitting elevated input cost volatility into an energy-intensive industry such as graphite electrodes and indirectly into downstream steel demand.
- Climate change, emissions and carbon-transition regulation — BRSR lists Climate Change and Emission Management as its first material issue - physical and transition risks including extreme weather, regulatory changes and rising carbon costs that may impact operations and increase compliance costs; mitigation includes hydrogen blending evaluation, a 2.4 MW solar addition, EVs, a furnace-oil-to-natural-gas conversion and the 15,000 MT expansion powered by natural gas. The Corporate Overview adds exposure to evolving global regulations and shifts in the carbon-border trade landscape.
- Geopolitical fragmentation, trade barriers and supply-chain realignment — The MD&A describes a move from efficiency-driven globalisation to resilience-led regionalisation, introducing a 'fragmentation premium' - higher logistics and sourcing costs, duplicated supply networks and increased working capital intensity - with downside risks skewed to escalating conflicts, prolonged energy price shocks and deepening trade fragmentation.
- Air emissions compliance — BRSR flags that uncontrolled air emissions can cause environmental degradation, health risks, regulatory non-compliance and reputational damage; mitigation includes monitoring systems plus electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers and baghouse filters installed as part of the 15,000 MT capacity expansion project.
- Water withdrawal and wastewater management — BRSR treats water as a critical industrial resource where unsustainable withdrawal and inadequate treatment can cause regulatory challenges, operational disruptions and environmental impacts; the Company operates ETPs, upgraded STPs and recycles treated wastewater, achieving Zero Liquid Discharge as certified by the Madhya Pradesh Pollution Control Board.
- Industrial waste handling and disposal — BRSR notes waste generation is inherent to manufacturing and that inefficient handling risks regulatory non-compliance, environmental liabilities and reputational damage; the Company disposes through authorised recyclers and is working towards zero waste to landfill by FY 2030.
- Occupational health and safety — BRSR flags inherent occupational hazards that may cause accidents, injuries or health impacts, with failure to maintain robust safety standards leading to legal liabilities, operational disruptions and reputational damage; mitigated through Factories Act 1948 compliance and ISO 45001:2018 implementation.
- Data privacy and cyber security — BRSR flags increasing reliance on digital systems exposing the Company to cybersecurity threats and data breaches, which could cause operational disruptions, financial losses, regulatory penalties and reputational damage.
- Human rights across operations and value chain — BRSR identifies potential human rights risks including labour practices and working conditions, where failure to identify and address them can lead to regulatory scrutiny, reputational damage and stakeholder concerns; a Human Rights Policy with due diligence processes is in place.
- Product stewardship and customer quality complaints — BRSR flags that products must meet evolving regulatory, environmental and customer expectations across their lifecycle, with inadequate stewardship causing non-compliance and reputational risk as sustainability considerations gain prominence in procurement. The complaints table shows 30 customer complaints filed in FY 2025-26 with 18 pending resolution at year end (50 filed and 45 pending in FY 2024-25), several awaiting customer-end evaluation of improved material.
- Economic performance and market volatility — BRSR treats sustained financial performance as both risk and opportunity, since adverse economic conditions or market volatility can impact profitability, liquidity and investor confidence; managed through cost discipline, risk frameworks and transparent reporting. The Board separately states that in its opinion there are no material risks that may threaten the existence of the Company.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body:
- **Graphite electrodes (HEG Ltd):** 100,000 TPA at a single location — by far the world's largest, against the next two largest plants at ~70,000 TPA each; expanding to 115,000 TPA by early 2028, widening the scale gap. Running >90%, exports 70-75%, present in 30+ countries. Middle East ~20% of sales; USA <10%.
- **TACC Limited (graphite anode):** 20,000 TPA under construction, ₹2,200-2,300cr capex, 40% spent, commercial production Q1 FY28, ~35% target EBITDA margin, 4-5 year payback; ₹1,240cr SBI debt secured. Phase 2 of 10,000t (~₹800cr) targeted for 2029; land supports 30,000t.
- **Bhilwara Energy (BEL):** two operating hydro plants totalling ~300MW, debt-free, throwing off ₹320-350cr of annual free cash flow. Run-of-river IPPs with 30-40% peaking power sold as high as ₹7-10/unit against ~₹4 for regular power, blending to ~₹5.5+. Statkraft's 49% of Malana Power bought in for ~₹1,200cr. Pipeline: 75MW hydro (~2029) and 300MW DC C&I solar (~18 months), together ~₹200cr incremental EBITDA.
- **HEG Advanced Materials / HEG Greentech:** the demerger vehicle. NCLT order reserved; separate investor call promised on pronouncement. Post-scheme ~32.9cr shares.
business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body:
- **Scale at a single location is the stated cost moat:** 100,000 TPA versus ~70,000 TPA for the next two largest plants globally, going to 115,000 TPA — "*its scale and cost-efficient operations place HEG among the most competitive producers globally*", and the Chairman's blunt claim, "*we will have a higher margin than anybody else.*"
- **Consolidated global industry structure.** "*There are only 3, 4 of us in the world*" outside China, which is why GrafTech's and Tokai's announced increases translate into a sector-wide price move HEG can follow rather than fight.
- **Utilisation gap versus Western peers.** HEG runs >90% while Western capacity utilisation is ~60-65% (per an analyst, uncontested) — evidence that HEG's market access, not capacity, is the binding constraint.
- **Geographic diversification as tariff insurance.** Exports across 30+ countries with no single dominant market means US anti-dumping/countervailing action on <10% of volume is absorbable: "*if something comes, which is totally unreasonable, it will not be difficult for us to absorb that volume elsewhere.*"
- **Balance sheet as an option.** Debt-free with ₹858cr treasury, funding a ₹2,200cr anode programme with only ₹1,240cr of project debt.

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers (listed names)

business.body:
- Largest graphite electrode plant in the Western world at 100,000 tonnes annual capacity, and among the top three producers globally excluding China, operating one of the industry's most modern facilities.
- High-technology, high-entry-barrier business: HEG was the last new entrant in the Western world, in 1976, and the deck notes no other Western company has announced additional capacity besides HEG's own.
- Graphite electrodes are a consumable for electric arc furnaces, acting as the electrical conductor that generates the heat to melt steel scrap, tying HEG's demand directly to EAF steel output.
- Deep customer entrenchment: a large portion of production goes to the world's top 20 steel companies, alongside long-standing raw-material partnerships with leading global suppliers.
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Industry runway] Per the OECD outlook, around 71 million tonnes of new EAF steelmaking capacity is planned globally between 2026 and 2028, the key long-term demand driver for graphite electrodes.
- [Demand outlook] The World Steel Association forecasts global steel demand growth of 0.3% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027, led by markets outside China; ex-China crude steel output rose 2.1% YoY in H1 2026 while total world output fell 0.7%.
- [India tailwind] India remains the fastest-growing large producer, with crude steel output up 7.1% YoY to 87 Mt in H1 2026 on infrastructure, construction and manufacturing demand.
- [Portfolio change] Consolidated statements show a discontinued operation that contributed profit through FY26 but nil in the June 2026 quarter, indicating a completed exit or separation the deck does not explain.
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: HEG Limited manufactures graphite electrodes, which accounted for 91.26% of turnover (NIC 23994), from a single large site at Mandideep near Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. Its clientele primarily comprises leading steel manufacturers operating Electric Arc Furnaces, with named customers including Jindal Steel and Power, SAIL, ArcelorMittal, Qatar Steel, Emirates Steel, Tata Steel, CELSA Group, Jindal Stainless and Acerinox Europia; it also supplies specialised graphite products to refractories, aluminium, chemical, electrochemical, power, cement and glass industries. The Company additionally holds captive power generation capacity of 86 MW (two thermal plants and a hydroelectric facility), reported as a separate Power segment, and is executing a composite scheme of arrangement that would separate the graphite business from its anode-materials/green-energy ambitions.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Graphite Electrodes:** Graphite electrodes (Ultra High Power segment, in which the Company states it is dominant), Specialised high-quality graphite products for non-steel industries
- **Power:** Captive thermal power (two plants), Hydroelectric power (sold through IEX and bipartite power purchase agreements with open access consumers)

latest_quarter.body: Standalone margin of 29% (vs 23% a year ago) on *lower* volumes — the drivers are realisation improvement (~7-8% price improvement in Q1 per a prior media interview), product and geographic mix, and the fact that **old, cheaper needle coke stock is still in the cost base**. That is the crux of the H2 setup: needle coke has risen $200-300/t since the Middle East disruption and adds roughly 10-15% to electrode cost, but 3-4 months of inventory plus a 3-4 month conversion cycle push the impact to November-January. HEG's own price increases start from October as the September/October book rolls off. Management would not quantify the net spread — "*rather than going into the specific number, which is very risky on a call*" — committing only to maintaining current margins. Energy costs and ocean freight are the other inflating inputs; management frames a price increase as an industry necessity rather than an opportunity: "*as an industry, we all need a price increase.*"
latest_quarter.title: Margins & cost dynamics

latest_quarter.body:
- **Q1 FY27 (this):** Standalone revenue ₹681cr (+11% YoY, +13% QoQ), EBITDA ₹211cr / 29% (vs ₹154cr / 23% YoY and **-₹126cr in Q4FY26**), PAT ₹110cr (+53% YoY, vs -₹163cr QoQ); consol EBITDA ₹194cr / 27%, PAT ₹122cr. Volumes *down*; utilisation >90% (91%); entire improvement from realisation, mix and legacy cheap needle coke. Q4's losses and Q1's ₹43cr other income both driven by mark-to-market on foreign equity investments. Debt-free, ₹858cr treasury. Guidance: utilisation 90-95% for FY27 with no headroom above 94-95%; margins to be maintained at ~28-29%; own price increases only from October (peers GrafTech $600-1,200/t, Tokai $930/t announced); needle coke +$200-300/t hits P&L Nov-Jan; 115,000 TPA electrode expansion by early 2028. Anode (TACC): production Q1 FY28, ₹600-700cr year-1 revenue at 40-50% utilisation → >₹1,200cr year 2 → ₹1,500-1,600cr year 3 at ~35% EBITDA margin, 4-5 year payback; 40% of ₹2,200cr capex spent; **70% of capacity to be contracted on 3-5 year Tier-1 deals within 1-1.5 months**; ~₹1,500cr gross debt by 31-Mar-27; phase 2 +10,000t at ₹800cr by 2029. Greentech: 300MW hydro throwing ₹320-350cr FCF, +300MW solar in 18 months, +75MW hydro by ~2029, ~₹200cr incremental EBITDA, **₹1,000cr+ EBITDA targeted by 2030**. Demerger: NCLT order **reserved**; post-scheme ~32.9cr shares.
- _Q2 FY27 → check: **70% of anode capacity contracted** (promised within 1-1.5 months of 24-Jul); NCLT order pronounced and record date announced; US CVD (end-July) and ADD (end-September) outcomes; utilisation staying >90%; margins holding at ~29% before the cost step-up; anode capex burn tracking to 90-95% of ₹2,200cr by end-FY27._
- _Q3 FY27 → the real test: **HEG's own October price increases realised** versus the **needle coke $200-300/t cost landing Nov-Jan**. The margin-maintenance promise is decided here, not in Q2._

outlook.body:
- **Utilisation: >90% in forthcoming quarters, closing FY27 between 90% and 95%** — with an explicit ceiling: "*there's no more headroom beyond 94% or 95%… because then you have to create ideal conditions to reach 100% and conditions are never ideal.*" Chairman's closing line: "*we will produce at 90%, 95% capacity utilisation come what may.*"
- **Margins: maintained at current levels.** Chairman declined a number then confirmed the ~28-29% (including other income) framing when pressed: "*we'll be able to maintain the margins that we are now talking about. And we will have a higher margin than anybody else.*"
- **Pricing: HEG's own increases only take effect from October** — the book is committed through September/October. New business is already being booked at higher prices. Peers have announced **GrafTech $600-1,200/t** (by size/quality) and **Tokai Carbon $930/t**; HEG will "follow suit" but expects nothing substantial in the next one to two quarters because the industry is broadly sold out.
- **Cost lag: needle coke increase of $200-300/t hits the P&L only towards Nov-Dec-Jan**, given 3-4 months of stock plus a 3-4 month conversion cycle. Needle coke is roughly **10-15% of electrode cost**.
- **Electrode capacity: expansion from 100,000 to 115,000 TPA is "on track" and "should be in operation by early 2028."**
- **Anode (TACC) — the most quantified guidance on the call:** commercial production starts **Q1 FY28**; year 1 at 40-50% utilisation → **revenue ₹600-700cr**; year 2 **>₹1,200cr**; year 3 **₹1,500-1,600cr**; **EBITDA margin ~35%** across all three years; **payback 4-5 years** on the ₹2,200cr capex.
- **Anode contracting: ~70% of the 20,000t capacity to be locked into 3-5 year contracts with Tier-1 global players "within the next 1, 1.5 months."**
- **Anode capex phasing:** ₹2,200-2,300cr total for 20,000t; **40% already spent**; 90-95% of payments by end-FY27, balance ~10% in Q1 FY28.
- **Anode phase 2:** a further **10,000t for ~₹800cr, decided immediately after the 20,000t completes, facility up by 2029** (land supports 30,000t). Full 30,000t programme ≈ ₹3,100cr, ~70% debt-financed.
- **TACC debt:** ₹1,240cr already secured from SBI; **~₹1,500cr gross debt expected on the 31-Mar-2027 balance sheet**; balance funded from own capital and internal accruals.
- **Bhilwara Energy / Greentech power:** 300MW of operating hydro, debt-free, generating **₹320-350cr free cash flow per year** at an assumed blended realisation of **~₹5.5/unit**; a **300MW DC C&I solar project in the next 18 months** and a **75MW hydro (acquired from Statkraft, ~30% of work already done) by ~2029 (2.5 years)**, together adding **~₹200cr of EBITDA**.
- **HEG Greentech: "by the year 2030, we should be aiming at a 4-digit EBITDA between all the businesses combined"** (i.e. ₹1,000cr+).
- **Demerger:** NCLT has **reserved its order**; timeline and record date to follow, plus a dedicated investor call on HEG Advanced Materials once pronounced. Post-scheme share count in the demerged entity ~**32.9cr shares** (from HEG's current ~19.7-19.8cr), with ~13cr new shares to Singularity, promoters and RSWM; **no further issuance thereafter**.
- **Malana/Statkraft acquisition debt** (~₹1,200cr paid, 50% commercial banks + family office + Bhilwara Energy; ₹600cr sitting in BEL's books via subsidiaries) to be **retired before the Greentech consolidation**.

outlook.body:
- Demerge into two distinct, focused listed entities under a composite scheme of arrangement filed with NCLT - the graphite electrode business (positioned as a global cost leader for the EAF super-cycle) and the HEG Greentech platform of energy-transition businesses - to give each entity independent access to capital, its own brand identity and a clean platform for future growth.
- Grow electrode capacity organically rather than by acquisition - 'build new, build right, and build in India' - because the Indian base offers cost competitiveness through scale, economical manpower and competitive power cost versus the Western world's old graphite electrode plants.
- Prefer brownfield expansion at Mandideep: it costs less than half the capital intensity of a greenfield plant, leverages surplus nipple capacity (the highest value-add component of the electrode) and deepens economies of scale at the world's largest single-location plant.
- Build HEG Greentech as India's first manufacturing-led, research-driven battery components and applications company across two divisions - advanced battery materials and battery solutions, and green power generation spanning hydro, solar, wind and BESS - owning the full ecosystem from hydro to advanced battery materials to battery EPC to independent power production.
- Enter advanced battery materials with a 20,000-tonne anode plant scaling to at least 60,000 tonnes by FY32, and commercialise an in-house graphene process (technical tests passed, patents filed) toward a 4,000 MT+ derivatives facility.
- Protect and grow liquidity: maintain the zero long-term debt position, the treasury and the GrafTech holding, which management describes as a powerful needle coke hedge providing 'staying power'.
- Remain attentive to margins and position to capture the operating leverage of an eventual industry-wide pricing recovery.
- Consolidate hydroelectric assets and move into anode materials, battery storage and renewable IPP capacity as coherent extensions of a single carbon-science identity serving the energy transition, with energy efficiency at Mandideep, water and waste stewardship, safety and community engagement stated as non-negotiable priorities.
- HEG's Dividend Distribution Policy, framed under SEBI LODR and approved by the Board, applies to its single class of equity shares. Members may expect dividend based on current year profits and the outlook in line with the internal and external environment, operating cash flows, funding of growth needs including working capital, capital expenditure and repayment of debt, dividend payout trends (payout ratio measured as dividend including dividend tax recommended for the year as a percentage of net profit for that year), tax implications on distribution, provision for unforeseen events and contingencies with financial implications, and any other factor the Board deems fit. The Board may declare interim dividend(s) as and when it considers fit and recommends the final dividend for Members' approval at the general meeting. For FY 2025-26 the Board recommended, and the AGM notice puts to Members, a final dividend of Rs 3.40 per equity share of face value Rs 2 each, payable to members on the register as at close of business on 22nd July 2026.
- Working towards zero waste to landfill by FY 2030, with responsible waste disposal through authorised recyclers
- Zero Liquid Discharge achieved and certified by the Madhya Pradesh Pollution Control Board, supported by fully functional Effluent Treatment Plants, upgraded Sewage Treatment Plants and reuse of treated wastewater for non-potable purposes
- Commissioning of a 2.4 MW solar power plant in addition to an existing 3 MW solar plant, as part of the decarbonisation strategy
- Planned conversion of furnaces and kilns from furnace oil to natural gas
- The 15,000 MT capacity expansion is designed to be powered by natural gas, and carries electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers and baghouse filters for particulate and gaseous emission control
- Evaluation of hydrogen blending with natural gas to reduce carbon intensity
- Adoption of electric vehicles for internal and intercity mobility (three EVs deployed), in-plant trucks and battery-operated forklifts to reduce diesel consumption
- Development of a long-term renewable energy roadmap within a comprehensive energy management framework
- ISO 45001:2018 Occupational Health and Safety Management System implemented, alongside Factories Act 1948 compliance
- Human Rights Policy supported by due diligence processes; Business Ethics Policy, Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, formal Grievance Redressal Policy, POSH Policy and Whistle Blower Policy in place
- Data protection frameworks aligned with global standards
- ESG reporting journey started in 2023-24 with formal evaluation of all metrics, an inaugural ESG Report (2023-24) and a 2024-25 ESG Report
- Enterprise Risk Management framework run on an annual cycle across five vectors (objective alignment, continuous identification, mitigation engineering, indicator monitoring, gap closure), with a Risk Management Committee constituted under SEBI LODR
- CSR: the Akshaya Patra mega kitchen at Bhopal - the first in Madhya Pradesh - with about 2.25 Crore+ meals served up to March 2026 and approximately 44,000 students across around 501 schools and madrasas enrolled under the Mid-Day Meal Programme
- CSR: farmer empowerment through Global Vikas Trust in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, stated to have impacted over 30,000 farmers with approximately 7.00 Crore trees planted and incomes improving 8 to 10 times
- CSR: the CBSE-affiliated Graphite School at Mandideep, Bhopal, run by a Company-funded trust for approximately 1,900 students
- Shri Manish Gulati, Executive Director, also acts as Chief Sustainability Officer, and a CSR & ESG Committee oversees CSR activities
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: HEG operates the world's largest single-site graphite electrode plant at Mandideep with an existing production capacity of 100,000 tonnes per annum, and is adding 15,000 tonnes at the same location to take total installed capacity to 115,000 tonnes per annum by early 2028. The Board approved this brownfield expansion at a capex of Rs 650 Crores; production is stated to commence in the first quarter of calendar year 2028, timed to the peak of the new EAF commissioning cycle. Management frames the choice as organic and brownfield by design - it costs less than half the capital intensity of a greenfield plant, leverages surplus nipple capacity (the highest value-add component of the electrode) and deepens economies of scale at the world's largest single-location plant; the Company says it will fund the entire Rs 650 Crore electrode expansion and the larger Greentech build-out without compromising the balance sheet. The new units are designed to operate exclusively on natural gas, and as part of the 15,000 MT expansion project advanced air pollution control systems (electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers and baghouse filters) have been installed. Beyond electrodes, the Chairman describes a proposed-to-be-listed HEG Greentech platform beginning with a 20,000-tonne anode plant scaling to at least 60,000 tonnes by FY32, a graphene derivatives facility scaling towards 4,000 MT+, and green power generation spanning hydro, solar, wind and BESS; these sit within a composite scheme of arrangement pending NCLT approval. On-site energy capex includes a 3 MW solar plant already operating with an additional 2.4 MW under commissioning and expected operational by June 2026, and a Rs 5 Crore approved capital expenditure to convert selected furnace oil-based burners to natural gas, with implementation planned in FY 2026-27. The Company also holds captive power generation capacity of 86 MW (two thermal power plants and a hydroelectric facility), with the thermal plants closed for most of 2025-26 on un-economical coal-power costs.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Structural migration of steelmaking from blast furnaces to the Electric Arc Furnace route - EAF steelmaking emits approximately one-fourth as much carbon - converted from an environmental preference into a financial necessity by Europe's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, the Tariff Rate Quota regime effective July 2026 and tightening regulations across major economies.
- More than 100 mmt of new greenfield EAF steelmaking capacity has been announced globally; approximately 21 mmt became operational between 2022 and 2025 and an additional 60 mmt is expected to come on stream between 2026 and 2028 (the Chairman states 60 million tonnes are under active construction with commissioning planned by 2028).
- The Company anticipates graphite electrode demand will gradually increase by 190,000-200,000 mt by 2030, against current Ultra High Power demand in ex-China markets of approximately 500,000-600,000 mt; the Chairman frames the same opportunity as 150,000 to 200,000 tonnes of incremental annual demand at a consumption ratio of 1.5 to 2 kilograms of electrodes per tonne of steel, almost entirely in the UHP segment.
- Supply cannot respond easily: no new company has entered the graphite electrode space since 1976 ex-China other than HEG's Mandideep facility, most Western capacity is more than 50 years old, and reactivating shuttered plants is prohibitively expensive.
- Pricing lever: management states that if ex-China utilisation approaches the 80-85% range the pricing environment could become more favourable for producers, and that HEG is best-placed to capture the operating leverage of that recovery; HEG ran above 90% utilisation while the global industry average was 60-65%.
- Needle coke prices remained stable during the year and are expected to remain at similar levels during the first half of FY 2025-26 (as printed in the Board's Report).
- China headwind: China's steel production fell 4.4% to 960.8 mmt while its exports rose 7.5% to a record 119 mmt in 2025 - up 78% over five years - exerting pressure on graphite electrode demand in global markets outside China.
- India's steel production rose 10.4% to 164.9 mmt, but Indian steel is predominantly blast-furnace route with a substantial induction-furnace share, which does not form part of the Company's customer base.
- Global steel demand is described as broadly stable at around 1.72 billion tonnes in 2025 and projected to grow marginally by ~0.3% in 2026, with the industry approaching the bottom of its cycle and a more visible recovery projected from 2027.
- Energy costs are the central transmission channel for an energy-intensive industry - elevated input cost volatility plus an indirect impact on downstream steel demand; electricity pricing is particularly critical for EAF-based production.
- Near-term conditions remain influenced by geopolitical tensions and trade disruptions from the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts, trade fragmentation, tariffs, safeguard duties and anti-dumping measures.
- Steel prices remained under pressure across most key consuming markets owing to subdued industrial and manufacturing activity, and pricing pressure persists in the graphite electrode industry.

The forward setup is unusually legible: GrafTech and Tokai have announced electrode price hikes of $600-1,200/t and $930/t respectively, HEG is booked through September/October so its own increases only bite from October, and needle coke (up $200-300/t) only hits the P&L in Nov-Jan — a favourable price-cost lag into H2.
